newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian politicians set to cooperate in Duma bid.
newsitem.headline: Russian politicians set to cooperate in Duma bid.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed gave his backing to the parliamentary ambitions of ousted presidential bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov on Sunday, heralding what could be a powerful alliance for the post-Yeltsin era.
Russian news agencies said Lebed, speaking in the arms manufacturing centre of Tula, promised to support Korzkakov's bid to stand there for election to the State Duma lower house of parliament.

"Alexander Lebed declared his intention to support... Alexander Korzhakov in his election campaign in the Tula region," Interfax news agency said. Lebed appealed to Tula residents to "make the right choice" in the election, it added.
The Tula seat, won by Lebed in a December parliamentary election, fell vacant after President Boris Yeltsin named Lebed his personal security adviser and secretary of the Security Council in June.

The president sacked the hawkish Korzhakov two days later, dumping a man who had been his tennis, swimming and -- some say -- drinking partner and then delighted Kremlin liberals by picking Korzhakov's political foe Anatoly Chubais as his chief of staff.
The stocky ex-bodyguard has made no secret of his dislike for liberal economist Chubais, accusing him of seizing the role of regent and acting in an unconstitutional way.
An alliance between Lebed and Korzhakov, who once controlled the vast presidential security service, could create a powerful force on the Russian political scene.

Lebed, a reserve paratroop general whose main boast in office is a tenuous peace deal in breakaway Chechnya, was popular on the hustings during the Russian presidential election, but he has few allies in the Kremlin.
Korzhakov, who was a Kremlin insider and a close Yeltsin ally for many years, has threatened to spill the beans about what he says is top-level corruption within the Kremlin.
He has denied allegations, made by a former top businessman, that he was involved in a multi-million-dollar extortion demand.

Korzhakov, 46, speaking at his first news conference on Friday, said Yeltsin's current entourage had run the president into the ground during the campaign and was now trying to manipulate events behind his back.
"What we have now is that power, in an apparently legitimate way, has gone into the hands of those never elected in a legitimate way," Korzhakov said, making clear he was referring to Chubais.
Chubais has not yet commented on Korzhakov's allegations.
Korzhakov said on Friday that Lebed had "the best political future in the country" but played down his own importance. A seat in the Duma would give him parliamentary immunity from any prosecution.
Lebed took third place in the June 16 first round of Russia's presidential election behind Yeltsin and communist Gennady Zyuganov, winning 15 percent of the vote.
He has made no secret of his presidential ambitions if Yeltsin dies or has to step down early because of ill health.

The president has spent few of the first 100 days of his second term in office in the Kremlin. He is currently in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where doctors are preparing him for bypass surgery to improve blood supply to the heart.
